utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Jason Antley for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no housekeeping matters, may the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, ma'am. Before counsel for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- the accused Stanisic continues his cross-examination, I would remind you, you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam. Madam, yesterday we mentioned the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was applied in 1992. So I would like to comment Article 153 with you. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, this is document which in this case is marked P120 and it's under tab 152 in the Defence binder. I will read out you to the text of Article 153, paragraph 1. It says: "The public prosecutor will refuse to deal with a criminal report if, from the -- if it follows from the criminal report that the offence committed" -- I apologise. I see here that the reference in the transcript is 152. However, I'm reading Article 153, paragraph 1. So I will continue: "... if it follows from the report itself that the act reported is not a criminal offence prosecuted ex officio, if the statute of limitation applies or if the act is covered by amnesty or pardon, or if there are other circumstances which make prosecution impossible, the public prosecutor will inform the injured party of the rejection of the criminal report and of the reasons for that within eight days, reference to Article 60, and if a body of the -- of the Ministry of Interior submitted the report, that body will also be informed." Do you remember that Article of the Law on Criminal Procedure, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain. If you, as a public prosecutor, for certain reasons establish that there are no grounds for initiating criminal procedure and reject the criminal report, then you are duty-bound to inform the injured party accordingly. The injured party in -- in every case. And if the criminal report was filed by the police, then both the injured party and the police must be informed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then, within the set deadline, I believe it was eight days, that injured party has the right to file an appropriate act with the court that has jurisdiction in the capacity of subsidiary prosecutor to initiate criminal proceedings, the -- although the criminal report was rejected by the public prosecutor's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After filing such an act, such a document, which was done by the injured party, then the court that has jurisdiction is duty-bound to act upon it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if I may explain. If the injured party within eight days from the reception of the notification by the public prosecutor, that criminal report so-and-so was rejected, so if the deadline was met, then the court will request from the public prosecutor that the case file be forwarded to them. I would like that -- that was an amendment because paragraph 1 does not outline what the prosecutor's office must do in such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. So the public prosecutor's office, upon the request of the court, submits the entire case file to the court if the injured party initiated criminal prosecution in the capacity of subsidiary prosecutor. Let me read to you paragraph 2 of Article 153. It says: "If ... the public prosecutor cannot draw conclusion based on the criminal report itself, if the alleged -- of the allegations in the criminal report are likely or if the information contained therein is -- doesn't constitute sufficient grounds for a decision whether an investigation must be launched, or, if the public prosecutor has only -- has hearsay evidence of the commitment of a criminal offence, especially if the perpetrator is unknown, then the public prosecutor, if he cannot do it himself or through other bodies, will request the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior to collect necessary information and take other measures to detect the criminal offence and its perpetrator. Reference to Articles 151 and Article 152." And now the last sentence: "The public prosecutor can always request the bodies of the Ministry of the Interior to inform him of the measures taken by them." Do you remember these provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in cases where -- let's envisage a certain scenario, the public prosecutor hears rumours that a criminal offence has been committed, then the public prosecutor will act himself and act autonomously, if he can. If not, he will request assistance from the police and other bodies to supply additional information to enable him to initiate criminal proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, as we have seen, apart from the right to make that request, you also have the right to request information on all measures taken by other bodies and services, with regard to your request; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me give some clarification. If the police doesn't act upon the request of the public prosecutor to collect information, and the public prosecutor sometimes requests urgent action or action within a set deadline, then the public prosecutor will make -- will send an urgent reminder to the police to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, yesterday we commented that, under the law, the police and all other agencies and services were duty-bound to act upon the request of the public prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. And if they don't do so, they are duty-bound to inform the public prosecutor of the reasons for that, failing to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I believe that now the Bench is better acquainted with the subject matter. I would like to interpret another provision for you. It's Article 18 from the Law on Public Prosecutor's Offices. That's document 1D04-2985. I said yesterday that once we get a translation of that law, we will insert it into the legal library, the law library. And it can you found under tab 153 of the Defence binder. So I'm about to read out Article 18: "A binding instruction as used in this law is considered to be instructions of general nature with regard to the work and the activities of public prosecutor's offices as well as instructions for taking action in individual cases." And it goes on to say: "Binding instructions of a general nature are issued by the public prosecutor of the Republic." Do you remember these provisions of Article 18, Madam?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, binding instructions of general nature are issued first and foremost by the public prosecutor of the Republic, we have just seen. And these are instructions of a general type that apply to all public prosecutor's offices in the territory where the -- the public prosecutor of that Republic has jurisdiction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and quite normally so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's in line with the hierarchy that's at the foundation of the institution of public prosecutor's offices; I agree with you. But apart from these binding instructions of general nature, there are also binding instructions for acting in individual cases, and perhaps we can illustrate this with an example. You, as a senior prosecutor, based on this provision, were able to give binding instructions to a subordinate prosecutor with regard to an entire case which he or she deals with; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law, yes; if there should be a need to issue such an instruction for the -- that particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree fully. So if there should be a need to do so. If you have information that makes it dissatisfied with the way your subordinate prosecutor deals with that case, you can issue a binding instruction to him or her and say you will qualify that offence as a serious offence or you will also indict additional persons, and so on and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Madam. Madam, I will now show you a document, P1318.23, which is in tab 156. This is a report on the work of the ministry and judicial organs for period May to October 1992, and it is dated 16 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we turn to page 2, please, both in the English and in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, what I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need the following page in the English version. In the Serbian version, we need the last paragraph, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see here it says, under 1: "Area of judiciary." And then in the third paragraph, underneath the title reads: "Judicial organs do not perform their functions with equal efficiency and usefulness. The Supreme Court and the republican public prosecutor's office have not begun to work yet, because" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to the following page in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: "Because the relevant personnel has not been elected or appointed, as yet, and the premises for these organs have not been found yet." And then they go on to explain the situation further. Is this your recollection also, that, in November, in mid-November of 1992, the office of the republican prosecutor of Republika Srpska had not yet started working?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I really don't know when the office of the republican prosecutor started working. I know when we, as the district prosecutor's office in Trebinje started working. As for the republican, I don't know the date. I know who the first republican prosecutor was, but I don't know when they started working. I'm simply not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us what is the name of the first republican prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Gladanjac, as far as I can remember. But I truly don't know when they started working, or when he started working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the district prosecutor's office in Trebinje where you worked as prosecutor, you said that you know the date. Can you please give us the date? You, yourself, were appointed on the 2nd of August. That's what you told us yesterday. What about the prosecutor's office in Trebinje? When did that office start working?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed on the 2nd of August as senior prosecutor, and deputies were appointed on that day as well. So the senior or higher prosecutor's office and the basic prosecutor's office were in the same building, and I think that around that time we started working immediately after the appointment, shortly thereafter. That's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, most likely, sometime in August of 1992, the office of the prosecutor started working, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could say so. A couple of days later, or 10 to 15 days later, thereabout.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the initiative launched by the Ministry of Justice and general administration of Republika Srpska in early summer of 1992, initiative aimed at taking over the responsibilities and jurisdiction of military courts by civilian courts. Are you familiar with that initiative?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska pointed out that there was serious problems in the work and in the process of establishing the rule of law, given that the military judiciary and military prosecutor's office were not functioning in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Madam, on page 19 of your statement, this is your statement of the 3rd and 5th of April, and the 2nd of June, paragraph 85, where you speak about the log-book of the basic prosecutor's office in Bijeljina. And you say: "In those log-book, I did not find a single criminal report for offences committed in the territory of Bijeljina municipality which would fall under the annex of the indictment." If you want, I can show you your statement.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need for that, I can remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the annexes to the indictment, not a single crime is listed from the territory of the basic public prosecutor's office in Bijeljina, except for the fact that the detention facility in Batkovici is mentioned. So I don't know to which crimes you were referring in paragraph 85 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps to refresh her memory. I mean, we did have appendix that lists by municipality all the crimes that she was looking for there in indictment. This came up with another witness, ST-210, if you want to bring that up. She can look at Bijeljina and see the types of crimes she was looking for that fell within the scope of the schedules of the indictment. I'm just offering this to assist in this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. Could Annex A be shown to the witness, Annex A of her statement. I don't know what number it has in e-court, unfortunately. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I can assist with that. It's under 65 ter 10528. That's where the two appendices are located and Appendice [sic] A is the one that contains all the crimes by municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. Again, we need the last page, where Bijeljina municipality is. Page 3 in e-court, in the Serbian version. I apologise, I apologise, ERN 06777865. It's most likely page 13 or 14. My math is not my strongest side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: See here, Madam, we have Bijeljina here, killing of at least, and so on, on the 24th of September, but as far as I know, we don't have this in our indictment. And then the next item is Batkovici detention facility, May to December 1992. When you gave your statement, is that what you were referring to in paragraph 85, these crimes? Is that what it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave my statement, I followed what was written under Bijeljina. September 1992, what's written there, and then what's written concerning Batkovici, and then I checked our log-book to see whether any entries were made that would match this. So this is the list that I was guided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't think it was your mistake at all. Now tell me, please, Madam, do you know that the camp for military prisoners of war was closed off for civilians. Civilians were banned from entering it. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about it, whether entry was allowed or banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that if it's a military camp for military prisoner of war, then it would be off-limits to everybody else except for authorised military personnel, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the regulations set forth, and regulations need to be abided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me, won't you, that in the military camp of military prisoners of war, if a crime is committed there, then a military prosecutor would have jurisdiction over that crime, rather than a civilian one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what the law stipulates, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you're not sure what the law says about these cases, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Military Courts, as far as I can remember now, lists item by item the crimes that the military courts have jurisdiction over. In addition to that, there is a provision setting forth that the military courts have jurisdiction for trials of prisoners of war, should they commit a crime. However, I'm not sure when this Law on Military courts entered into force. As soon as it did enter into force and as soon as military courts were set up, they naturally had jurisdiction over such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You must know that in the former SFRY there was a Law on Military Courts, Law on Military Prosecutor's Office, and the entire organisation of the military judiciary organs, the Law on Military Courts of the SFRY dates back to 1987 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is P1284.07.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the law was adopted in 1977, the Law on Military Courts, shortly after the Criminal Code of the SFRY was adopted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that's how it was, that the Law on Military Courts was also adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that Republika Srpska took over all regulations of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which were not contrary to the interests of the Republika Srpska and its people. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to give a very brief explanation. I'm not sure about this, whether the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska was simply renamed. Because previously we had the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they took it over with just renaming it. That applies to the general portion, as far as I can remember. So the Law on Criminal Procedure remained unchanged for a while. We had the general portion and then, in addition to that, we also had the Criminal Code which was taken over and that was the former Criminal Code of the SFRY. Now, as for the Law on Criminal Procedure, it was also taken over without any amendments. The Law on -- on Military Courts was, I think, also published in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska and that law listed specifically the offences for which the military courts had jurisdiction. That is to say, that these offences were not covered by other courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have just a couple of general questions. In relation to the documents that you went over - KT, KTN and KTA log-books - if my calculations are right, you went over log-books of 17 basic prosecutor's offices and two senior prosecutor's offices, one in Doboj and one in Banja Luka. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I also went over the Trebinje log-books. I think I also checked Trebinje, Doboj, and Banja Luka; but in Trebinje, there were no entries, relevant entries, so I did not enter any data into annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement and in the annexes to your statement, you dealt with the KTA log-books in cases where the injured parties were non-Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could infer from the information contained in the log-books that somebody was a non-Serb. It wasn't always legible or the name of the injured party wasn't always entered. So as far as I could reconstruct from the information available, I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the problem with reviewing these log-books lies with the fact that you must take for granted what was entered. You must rely on the person who entered the information so that much information can be missing, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, the information required was entered column by column, who filed the criminal report, when, the number of the file, who the injured party was, the place and date of the offence, et cetera. We tried to come up with some of this information subsequently. That's why there are also these annexes. For the information to be as complete as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you said a minute ago that you established that in some cases the information was illegible or possibly there was no reference to the injured party, et cetera; isn't that correct? You said so a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is why these cases were entered in table 4 where there are cases where we need additional information. Wherever something was unclear, we entered the relevant information in table 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I have a technical question now. In accordance with the usual way, or usual methodology of work in public prosecutor's offices, the reports that are received and entered into the KT log-book, that is, against a known perpetrator as well as those entered into the KTN log-book against unknown perpetrators, also considering the KTA log-book, in principle, you would always open a case file and you would ... for -- open a case file at the public prosecutor's offices for each such case, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done that way, and it had to be done that way. It was well-known where information about a case must be entered. If it -- something was entered in the KTA log-book of onsite investigations and later on a criminal report against a known or unknown perpetrator is filed, then the document -- documents would be transferred to the other log-book, depending on whether the perpetrator was known or unknown. So KTA was transferred to KTN, or KT, or was transferred to KTM, in case of a minor. We spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Tell me, Madam, yesterday when I was reviewing your amended statement and compared it to your previous findings, I found the following: In Sanski Most - you may remember because it's kind of a characteristic occurrence - a -- a file about a criminal offence was transferred to the military prosecutor's office concerning one Danilusko Kajtez?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and I did have that case file, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But while you were reviewing these log-books, did you have access to the log-books of the public prosecutor -- sorry. Military prosecutor's offices or the prosecutor's offices with military commands, or were they -- or -- or were you familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is correct. I also reviewed the log-books of the basic and district prosecutor's offices. I remember that even in the log-book there's an entry about the file having been transferred to the military prosecutor's office. Every log-book contains a box for possible transfers of the case file, and you must enter the relevant information there whether or not the case file was transferred to another prosecutor's office, civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Madam, let me ask you once more to provide concise answers so -- for it to be more easily understandable. And I see that your previous answer was not recorded fully or correctly. So let me repeat. While you were reviewing the log-books, you reviewed a total of 17 log-books of basic prosecutor's offices, civilian offices, and two -- that is, three log-books of higher or senior civilian prosecutor's offices, but you did not review any log-book of a senior or supreme military prosecutor's office with any military command for the relevant period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that it was correct. I did not review military log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, your experience as a prosecutor goes back to 1976 when you started working at the basic public prosecutor's office in Trebinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you have experience as a prosecutor, from 1976 to 1992, then you were also prosecutor during the war and you have been one since the end of the war, tell me about the following: The situation with regard to criminal offences committed in the territory of -- under the jurisdiction of your basic prosecutor's office, first and foremost, but then also for the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1976 till the 1990s, it is striking that there was a small number of serious crimes committed; isn't -- isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that in the territory under the jurisdiction of the basic prosecutor's office in Trebinje, until 1992, the -- most offences were minor offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we spoke before your testimony in the presence of a colleague from the OTP, I think that you told me that the average for the region of eastern Herzegovina was below one murder per year; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put forward that figure, and I agree that probably there was less than one murder per year. Murders were a rare occurrence in Trebinje. That is, in the territory covered -- under the jurisdiction of our prosecutor's office. Although we didn't have subject matter prosecution -- subject matter jurisdiction over murders. That lay with the prosecutor's office in Mostar, the senior prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us return to 1992. In 1992, if I understood you correctly, you worked for the public prosecutor's office in Trebinje; but, for a while, after the beginning of -- of the war, you lived in Bileca, and you travelled to work to Trebinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said during our conversation that I had fled for a short while. When there was shelling even close to the building where I lived and part of the apartment was damaged by shrapnel, I fled to Bileca and stayed there for a while but I came to work regularly and did my work. So I cannot really say that I lived outside of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "shelling," you mean shelling by the Croatian army, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know who shelled us, but I knew that shells fell in the city. One landed in the yard of the building where I lived, and one vehicle was destroyed. But I have no reliable information as to where the shells had come from, and I didn't inquire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As a higher prosecutor, or senior prosecutor in Trebinje, your subordinate prosecutor's offices were those in Bileca, Gacko, Ljubinje, Nevesinje, and you said Foca for a while, if I remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said municipalities. The senior public prosecutor's offices in Trebinje had three subordinate prosecutor's offices. The one in Trebinje, the one in Nevesinje, and the one in Foca. However, the basic public prosecutor's office in Nevesinje may not have started working at the same time as those in Foca and Trebinje. I am not sure, because I don't remember all the details. So these are the three prosecutor's offices. Whereas, as far as the municipalities are concerned, each municipality came under the jurisdiction of a certain basic prosecutor's office. If you're interested in the details, I can provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested only in the municipalities that are relevant for this indictment, and they are the municipalities of Gacko and Bileca. They were under your jurisdiction, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic public prosecutor's office in Trebinje had jurisdiction over the municipalities of Trebinje, Berkovici, Bileca, Ljubinje -- yes, Ljubinje. These are the municipalities that were under the jurisdiction of the basic public prosecutor's office of Trebinje. The one in Nevesinje covered Gacko, Nevesinje, and the Serbian municipality of Mostar. I don't know how large that is. And these are the municipalities or parts of municipalities covered by the basic public prosecutor's office in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, the municipal prosecutor's office in Nevesinje also had jurisdiction over the municipality of Gacko. But a minute ago you said that you were not sure when the municipal prosecutor's office in Nevesinje started working and that you allow for the possibility that it was only months after you had established the senior prosecutor's office -- or, rather, you were appointed senior prosecutor in Trebinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about maybe a month or two weeks. As far as I remember, on the same date the prosecutors in both the senior and the basic prosecutor's office in Trebinje were appointed. But I don't think that it was done at the same time for Nevesinje, for the reason that I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, Madam, both the basic prosecutor's office in Nevesinje and the basic prosecutor's office in Trebinje, both were subordinate to the senior prosecutor's in Trebinje headed by you in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We've seen that the public prosecutor's office of the Republic, we have seen -- that's what we saw on the documents that I showed you today, hadn't started working even in November 1992. It was basically you, as senior prosecutor in Trebinje, who held the highest prosecutorial position in eastern Herzegovina in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were giving your statement in March 2006, if you remember, the investigator of the OTP asked you about some locations where, allegedly, crimes had been committed in the area. Specifically the detention facility, hotel -- the hotel near the power plant in Gacko. Then the detention facility in the SJB building in Gacko. Then the detention facility in the SJB building in Bileca. Then the student's hostel in Bileca. Then the Mosa Pijade Barracks. And if that is recorded correctly in your statement, then you said that you knew nothing about the alleged crimes, that you had hadn't seen or heard anything about them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was recorded correctly. I didn't know and I didn't hear anything about it. I didn't hear about it until 1998 perhaps, and I didn't know until then, and later on, I found out. So I just wanted to be as specific as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Given that at that point in time you were -- you held the position of the senior prosecutor, there must have been -- or, rather, had there been a report filed by an injured party or by any civilians, or had the prosecutor's office received rumours about any grave crimes committed, you would have known about it. You would have been notified, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said earlier, the jurisdiction of the senior prosecutor's office in Trebinje, as well as all other senior prosecutor's offices, were only second-instance cases, appeals from lower courts covered by that office. As for the criminal reports, during that time we did not receive any criminal reports. I have not heard from deputies or from basic prosecutors either about them receiving such reports. They did not even come to me, asking me for advice about what to do in such cases. There was none of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question focussed on something quite specific. Do you know whether any of the citizens, any of injured parties, filed criminal reports for such or similar crimes to any of the basic prosecutor's offices which were under your jurisdiction in 1992? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information. I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Basic public prosecutor's offices, or you, as senior prosecutor, did any of you know of such or similar cases which would perhaps be registered in the KTA log-books? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know -- I did not know about this myself, and I received no such information from my subordinate prosecutors, basic public prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Had you learned of it, you or any other employee of the prosecutor's office, according to the law, you were duty-bound to launch criminal proceedings, based on the information you received; or, as we saw earlier, you were duty-bound to order certain organs or organs of the interior to collect relevant information; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have acted in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure. We certainly would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you held the highest prosecutorial position in eastern Herzegovina in 1992, did anybody come and complain to you about the work of prosecutor's offices, complained about them not doing their work, on not doing it properly? Such as giving preferential treatment to some individuals and persecuting some other individuals? Did you have any complaints of this nature?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the district public prosecutor's office, we never received any complaint, be it in writing or verbal, complaints of the nature that you described where somebody was complaining about the work of a prosecutor in the jurisdiction covered by the senior prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports or complaints that prosecutor's offices subordinated to you are guilty of discriminating on ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear, or did you ever receive, instructions or policy views saying that the prosecutor's offices, in their work, should discriminate on an ethnic basis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since the republican prosecutor's office did not work at that time, if prosecutor's offices subordinate to you had received such an instruction, then that instruction could have only come from you, as the highest prosecutors in that area, the senior prosecutors? I'm just giving you a theoretical, hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been very unusual in my mind that anybody from the judicial organs or from the justice system would write such an instruction. We never received anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on page 14 of your interview, dated 30th of March 2006, when asked by the Prosecutor whether there were certain complaints or objections raised in reference to the work of police, complaints addressed to you, as senior prosecutor, you said that you never ever received such complaints or objections from anyone in 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying that, and it is true, that neither in 1992 or in subsequent years, did I receive any such complaints or objections from anyone, including authorised officials. Even though, under the Law on Criminal Procedure, and that was a distinct possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you said something different from what you said. It says here that did you not receive such complaints or objections from anyone, including authorised officials. And I think that you said that you did not receive any complaints or objections of that nature, complaints or objections concerning the work of authorised officials; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify. I did not receive a single complaint concerning the work of authorised officials, police stations, or CSBs, which came under the jurisdiction of the senior prosecutor's office in Trebinje. I don't know whether I made myself clear now. This is entirely correct, because any such complaint or objection would have been recorded as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have just one more question. During your work in the prosecutor's office of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, before 1992, you must have gone to various professional seminars and work-shops organised for prosecutors and courts, right? Organised every year.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, up until 1992, it was done within the former Yugoslavia. So, to the extent that our funding allowed it, I did go to such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those were work-shops and seminars organised for civilian courts and civilian prosecutors, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that colleagues from civilian courts and civilian prosecutors were there. Now, whether there were any military ones as well, I really wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, whether, at any such professional conferences or seminars, there was discussion or exchange of opinions on prosecuting for crimes under chapter 16 of the Criminal Code of SFRY, which pertains for -- to war crimes and crime against humanity. Do you remember whether this was ever discussed at such professional gatherings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no. We typically discussed the current topics at the time and the current problems we encountered in our work at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Gacinovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Aleksandar Aleksic will cross-examine this witness. [Indiscernible] the Registry and legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Given that this is the first time I'm addressing this Chamber, I would like to say that it's a honour for me to be -- to participate in such a large case, and to be a member of Defence of Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Gacinovic. I will try not to repeat any of the issues or laws you covered with Mr. Zecevic, but we may have to touch upon some of those issues, in order to clarify some things. Yesterday, on pages 49, 50, and 51 of the transcript, you discussed with Mr. Zecevic provisions of Article 155 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, where it says that the public prosecutor's office can request that certain investigative activities be conducted even when the perpetrator is unknown. Then further on, that, an investigative judge can object to such a request, can disagree with it, and that, in that case, a trial chamber from Article 23 of the Law on Criminal Procedure would rule on that issue. And such a chamber would normally have three professional judges. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to follow up with a question. In such a situation -- or, rather, in a situation where investigative judge does not object to this request by the public prosecutor to carry out certain investigative activities, or if the Trial Chamber should rule that there's no basis for such a rejection or refusal on the part of the investigative judge, then such an investigative judge is duty-bound to act upon the request of the prosecutor and conduct all investigative steps requested.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure. I lost concentration for a moment. You said that if the Chamber should rule against the investigative judge, then the investigative judge is duty-bound to act upon the prosecutor's request. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And he is also duty-bound to do any other steps as required in the profession, to take statements, interview potential witnesses, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add to that. Should the Chamber overrule the disagreement on the part of the investigative judge, then the case file would go back to the investigative judge who was duty-bound do act upon the request of the prosecutor. However, when the request for individual investigative steps is made, the prosecutor always puts in that there's a request for the judge to carry out any other additional investigative activities that seem to be relevant, needed and so on, not just the ones specifically listed in the prosecutor's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. Once the investigative judge concludes the investigation and investigative activities which were initiated under Article 155, then the case file would be sent to public prosecutor for him to review it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the prosecutor would normally always put an instruction that once everything is concluded and completed, the case file should be returned to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now, in a situation where the investigative judge does not fully act in accordance with the request of the prosecutor, under Article 155, for example, what if the prosecutor proposed that ten persons be interviewed and the judge interviews only five of them. In such a case, did the public prosecutor have right and was he entitled to return the case file back to the judge to have additional investigative activities carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things are possible in such a situation. For example, out of nine proposed witnesses, the judge could interview only five but those five would be sufficient to elucidate the situation based on which the prosecutor can make a decision. In such a case, the prosecutor would not send back the case file to the judge. However, if the interview of those five witnesses not sufficient and the interviewing of additional four witnesses is needed, then the prosecutor could make a proposal to carry out additional investigative activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, before you proceed with your next question, perhaps this would be a convenient time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Witness, we won't dwell much longer on the Law on Criminal Procedure, but I have a few concluding questions. According to that law, when the perpetrator is known, it is standard procedure to have the person indicted, heard, if accessible to the court, and then a decision on investigation is issued followed by a number of other measures, such as witness interviews, expert analyses and investigative measures in general; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is not, according to the shortened procedure, then my answer is yes, if it is a full investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that law for now. Can you tell me something about the procedure of keeping public prosecutors' log-books. In terms of calendar years, is there an interruption after one year ends and the other one begins, in order to produce annual statistical reports?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each year the log-books start anew, from number one. On one sheet, it concerns the KT log-book, recording reports against known perpetrators. Each such a sheet would contain ten persons. It could so happen that there were four reports on a single sheet encompassing ten persons. It may happen, though, that the list does not start with the 1st of January, if the person in question is still in detention. For example, there may be no entries for five to ten days, but once a file is received by the prosecutor, it is stamped and it -- entered into the log-book as of that date. As for the end of each year, it sometimes happens that the last date is the 20th or the 25th of December. However, if a file has arrived by the 30th of December, it is stamped by the prosecutor's office. The rest is left as is, as on the 20th or the 25th of that year because of the break needed to produce such annual reports. In any case, all cases are entered, depending on the date received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Zecevic, touched upon the topic of case files containing each and every file. Can you just tell us what is between the different sides of the cover sheet? What is contained in each such file?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases of adult known perpetrators, on the first -- or cover page, it states Republika Srpska, basic prosecutor's office, or higher prosecutor's office, as well as the KT case number/year. Towards the middle, it says cover sheet and then it is followed by against, or file against what person, and the type of crime. In the right-hand side corner, it says the public prosecutor, together with the name of the person in question. On the left-hand side, archival dates or up to what date such a file would be kept. Inside, there would be a date of reception and what was done as part of that case file. If there was a request for an investigation, it would -- included in the file. And there is also a note forwarded to court, if this was the case, and any decisions by the judge are mentioned. We have the date of the investigation began, the day the investigation ended, when the indictment was raised, as well as all other dates and measures taken, including possible judgements, appeal, et cetera. This is regarding the KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, where are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only one or two questions left on this topic. When we heard several witnesses before, without going into names, the same people stated that for one to have a full view of the cases we need to have the case file cover. The witness now specified the details mentioned therein. This is the thrust of my question, and I have only one question left in that regard. Concerning P1567, this is what the focus of my questions was. I won't go into any details now before the witness, but it was referred to by some other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, with all due respect, I think we have been looking into possibly each and every aspect of the log-books that we possibly could. We have seen them, we have admitted some of them into evidence, we have been back and forth. Several witnesses have testified about it. And you are entering into an avenue of detail which I really think is superfluous and unnecessary at this stage. So I would strongly urge to you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand you, and I will do so. However, it was the Prosecutor who proposed this type of evidence. We didn't bring this witness and not only this witness -- in any case, I understand your view and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Learned colleague, you mentioned the necessary notifications, and let us not go into any legal details. But tell me this, when the competent prosecutor is asking the police for necessary notifications does the competent prosecutor do that with regard to any police station which he or she believes may provide it? Provide such information to him.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It means, in your case for example, you, as the senior public prosecutor in Trebinje, since the CSB was there, if you required some information from Bileca and Nevesinje, you and your junior prosecutors could turn directly to the stations in Bileca and Nevesinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was saying that it covers the entire area covered by the prosecutor's office. If there is something happening in one place, then information could be requested from another place and it would be processed as such. There shouldn't be any obstacles in that regard, and information could be sought from local police stations, as far as I recall. It could also be forwarded to the police station of Trebinje. In any case, the only important thing was to have the job done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: As far as the legal qualifications of a crime are concerned, would you agree with me that a public prosecutor, when receiving a criminal report, does not need to abide by that legal qualification. Also, the court dealing with the case does not need to follow the legal qualification of the crime concerned offered by the prosecutor. They need to qualify that decision based on the facts before them.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The prosecutor need not abide by the legal qualification offered. As for the judges, they have the same discretion, provided that there is no -- there are no facts on file which would indicated that it was actually a different type of crime that is at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I believe we may return to this issue later on, if we have time left. You were elected senior public prosecutor in Trebinje in August, the 2nd of August, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Were there general elections for prosecutor -- prosecutors and judges held at that time? Were there other people elected to those positions across the territory of the RS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I recall the area of Trebinje that this was the case. I recall the area of Trebinje. It has to do with the basic court, the county court, and the basic prosecutor's office. As for any other areas, there isn't much I can tell you. But it is most likely as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: At that time when you were elected, and up until late 1992, could one travel from eastern Herzegovina for example, from Trebinje, to the area of Banja Luka, Bosanska Krajina and other municipalities in that area? And did you travel there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I can only tell you about my experience. At the county prosecutor's office in Trebinje, we did not have a vehicle at our disposal and basically there wasn't any need for us to travel anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There is perhaps an uncertainty in the translation here. But I read in the transcript where the general elections for prosecutor as your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct. It is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, can you clarify "general elections."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I was going to raise the same issue on my re-examination. I don't think it is in dispute here that back in 1992 all judges were appointed by the Assembly at RS levels, so I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think it is a simple translation issue. Isn't it, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Learned colleague, you didn't know in what conditions the basic and county prosecutor's offices had to work in the area of Bosanska Krajina, Banja Luka, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, et cetera. In terms of personnel and such necessities as electricity, telephone lines and mail, you have no direct information or knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information regarding that, and basically there was no need for me to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. So as not to waste too much time, concerning your corrected statement and the annexes, I wanted to use the sample of the basic prosecutor's office in Teslic. In your statement, paragraph 23 - the latest statement - you say that you came across five crime entries where the injured parties were Serbs, whereas, the other side were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I can recall now, although to tell you anything more precise than that, I would have to refer to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I believe you can take my word for it. Those entries are at page 35 of that statement. The perpetrators referred to in these entries are Mile Stanojevic, Marijanovic, Stanko, et al, Aleksandar Kalicovic, Zeljko Tomic and Milenkovic, Radivoje. If you wish to peruse it, I can have that placed on the screen for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps to speed this up, we just hand her a copy of her annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: It will be the best way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just for the record, it's revised Annex 9 that she'll be looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document please be put on the screen for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you agree? You must give an oral answer.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see Exhibit 2D98, which is under tab 12 in the Zupljanin Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do take a look at the document on the screen, please. It's a criminal report filed by the SJB of Teslic on 24 December 1992 against, as far as can I tell by looking at it, four persons, Dalibor Djuric, Zdravko Aleksic, Jovo Petrovic, and Sladjan Cvijetic. Could I please ask you to look at the document on the screen. And you can compare what you see there to what you did later. And at the bottom of page 1, it says there are reasonable grounds to suspect that on 2 December 1992 they committed an armed robbery, which is on page 2 of the English translation. In the Serbian version, on page 2, which is also page 2 in English, it says that the crime was committed by entering houses, shooting through doors, and took some things, threatening people with firearms. The injured parties are -- are Razija Dzojic and Smajo Garic and some others. If you have trouble reading it, maybe we can enlarge it. Can you confirm what I have said so far, that, in this criminal report, four persons of Serb ethnicity are mentioned as perpetrators, as in the description of the crime four non-Serbs are mentioned as injured parties. Can you confirm that, and the crime in question is armed robbery?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And that the offence was committed on 2 December 1992, which means within the relevant period. So, Madam, I'm not trying to say that you are -- did something wrong. I'm merely saying that this particular criminal report did not figure in the log-book given to you to work with. Do you agree with that? And it cannot be found in your table either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wondering if the Defence could provide a KT entry number for this particular case. The reason I ask is -- he is asking a question that leaves open more or less an unanswered assertion. Did she miss this from the log-book or did the log-books not include it? I mean, there is not a stamp on this document saying that it was received by the prosecutor's office. I think that, you know, the witness should be entitled to review the log-book and determine whether it actually is in there, and it is unclear what the Defence's position is on that. If he can give us a KT entry number, then we can always cross-reference it to the log-book and see if there's an entry for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't say that it was in the log-book, that it was entered. I merely said that the log-book - now I'm stating my case - that the log-book is unreliable. I'm not saying that the witness didn't work well. I merely -- my case is that the log-book isn't reliable enough for us to get a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suspected that that was the purpose of your question. But isn't the objection or observation that Mr. Olmsted has made is that, without more, the witness is -- as it were, left at sea, in terms of trying to say -- to -- to connect this with anything at all. And without just being shown it, to be able to -- to be expected to answer in the witness box without having the -- having had the ability to herself to determine its inclusion or otherwise, in the log-book. Isn't it, at the end of the day, not very -- in a sense, almost unfair to the witness and not very helpful to the Chamber. Unless I'm missing something, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may just jump in very quickly. I will note that the Teslic log-books are in evidence, and therefore the Defence, at time of argument, can review the log-books and tell us or assert whether there is an entry for this particular case or no. We don't need this witness here to do that. If they want to take this course, it would require us to take probably a 30-minute recess, hand about a thousand pages of log-book for her to quickly review to determine whether this particular case was in that log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will move on to another topic. Could we please see 65 ter 2758 from e-court, please, which is P1361, item 0 -- or .06.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this exhibit yesterday during the examination-in-chief. This case is included in your overview, so I moved on to something else. I believe that you saw the entire file, didn't you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So this is a request to conduct an investigation submitted by the -- by the public prosecutor's office in Teslic against 16 persons for the most serious crimes. That is, the Mice case, as it is widely known. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entry 149/92 in the KT log-book, and it's tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. So please take a look at the bottom of page 5 in the Serbian version and then the entire page 6. In English, the relevant pages are 5, 6, and 7. In that part of the document, we can see the proposals made by the prosecutor to the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 6 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you see? These are proposals to examine witnesses. And if I am not mistaken, we're speaking about 52 witnesses in all here. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, the prosecutor, having received the criminal report, which is entered, and there's also the date of the report and against whom it is being filed, and the prosecutor also stated the date of the request to launch an investigation, so none of that is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see page 7 in the Serbian which is probably also page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you see item 5, Roman V, the Roman numeral V, where it says that the public prosecutor proposes that detention be ordered for all the accused pursuant to Article 191, paragraph 2, items 2 and 4 of the Law on Criminal Procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And to avoid further reference to the Articles of the Law on Criminal Procedure, do you agree with me when I say that item 2 is based on the fear that the accused, if they remain at large, will interfere with witnesses and with the course of justice. And that with regard to the circumstances of the commitment of the crimes, the public would be upset and weren't. And the -- these crimes are punished by ten years in prison or more?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember the provision on the Law on Criminal Procedure with regard to ordering detention, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see 2D88, which is tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: This is about the same case. This is a document of the basic court in Teslic dated 21 July, and it says that the investigating judge releases the aforementioned persons from detention, and detention was ordered ten days earlier. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what follows from this ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 of this document, both in Serbian and in English. Page 2. Can we enlarge it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph on this page, we read that the public prosecutor of Teslic agreed to release the individuals named in the disposition from custody; is that correct? And in the following paragraph, we read that the court particularly considered the request put forward by -- some military command and concluded that the accused would not be able to impact criminal proceedings by influencing witnesses who have not yet been examined. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. But I'm not here to give opinion about court rulings or proposals submitted by public prosecutors, and so on. As far as I understood, I came here to speak about what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But, Madam, earlier you spoke to Mr. Zecevic about binding instructions and authorisations -- or, rather, the powers that you as senior prosecutor had over subordinate prosecutors and so on. This is what I'd like to discuss with you. Here in this case, on 11 July, a request to launch an investigation was filed, and 52 witnesses were -- were supposed to be examined because there were many indictees. And it follows from this ruling that many witnesses were not examined, and detention had been ordered based on items 2 and 4. And the public prosecutor accepted that and acted in accordance. Isn't this a flagrant example of unlawful behaviour of a public prosecutor and an investigating judge? Detention was cancelled after ten days without a large number of witnesses having been examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Assuming, Mr. Aleksic, that the witness is able to answer that question, what is the relevance of that to -- to our proceedings? Apart, as the witness answered in your previous question, the purpose for which she was called. I suppose outside of that you're permitted to explore her credibility and whatnot, but the motive of the -- or competence of the prosecutor in a particular case, how is that of assistance? JUDGE HARHOFF, And, anyway, the document is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and, Your Honours, I don't think the Criminal Procedure Code is in question here. And this witness has no personal knowledge of this case. So how can she give an opinion as to whether the prosecutor in Teslic, in 1992, was doing his job or not or anything else unless she has time to review through the entire case with file, get familiar with it, get familiar with the facts of the case and then give an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do agree that the reason this witness came here was to go over the log-books, as requested by the Prosecutor. However, this witness has worked as a prosecutor for 35 years, and she answered questions of Mr. Zecevic concerning the powers and authorities of public prosecutor and what could possibly be done in a particular case. Based on her entire professional experience, I asked her to give me an answer in this case, and if the Chamber should want us to move on, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I simply wanted to say that I know what I would have done in a particular case, and I can tell you what I would have done as a prosecutor. I would have not acted in this way, and if any of my junior prosecutors did something like this, I know what I would have done. But as I sit here now, I cannot assess the work of the prosecutor in Teslic. It is not my job here to give comment on particular cases. I came here to provide information and insert it into tables, as requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gacinovic. Yes, Mr. Aleksic, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if we can summarise as follows: As you have said to Mr. Zecevic, you did not go over the log-books of military courts and military prosecutors, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You also didn't go over log-books concerning minors.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You also didn't go over cases, be it cases of courts or cases of prosecutors, except for the very limited number of cases provided to you by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Only where needed, where we couldn't conclude anything based on the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the quality of log-books and data entered into log-books is something that depends on -- or that is subject to human error, because these log-books are filled out by humans, by clerks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What sort of question is this, really, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in dozen instances or so, the witness, in her statement, said that in particular cases it could not be established who the perpetrator was due to insufficient information in log-books and that a clear picture would only be obtained if one looked into the entire case file, both cases of courts and cases of prosecutors. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was once chastised by this Trial Chamber for asking a question that begged common sense, and I think human error is present in everything, so I don't -- I agree with Judge Harhoff that this doesn't need to be pursued further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if I may add, I think this evidence has already been brought to the Court two or three times on exactly the same point, so I think we can skip it for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to you. I am a recent arrival, relevant recent arrival in this case, so it is probably my mistake. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Madam, based on everything you discussed with Mr. Zecevic and me, would you agree with me that log-books, on their own, are insufficient to gain a complete picture of how things were during this period of time, how the prosecutors' offices, courts, and police, worked from the 1st of April until the 31st of December; and that in order to have a complete analysis, one would need to have everything else that you lacked in this case, namely, information from the military court, military prosecutor's office, et cetera. That one would need all of that in order to have a complete and accurate picture?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I worked on this task, when it came to log-books that did not have complete data, all of that was reflected in table 4. If one wanted to have a complete picture about all of the crimes committed, then, naturally, one would need to have all of the log-books of the military prosecutor's office and all other prosecutor offices to have a realistic picture for the entire territory. As for the log-books that I analysed, in a lot of instances we came across data indicating that some of the cases reported to the basic prosecutor's office were later transferred to the military prosecutor's office, and I marked that particular information in relevant tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gacinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honours I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to go back first, Ms. Gacinovic, to a question that was raised by Mr. Zecevic today. He was asking you questions about Article 153 of the Criminal Procedure Code, if you may recall, and he phrased his question as such: If a prosecutor hears a rumour that a criminal offence was committed, the prosecutor will act himself and act autonomously, if he can. Can you tell us, back in 1992, did the prosecutor have the means, the resources, to investigate a criminal offence, to locate a perpetrator, to collect evidence at this pre-trial phase?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Olmsted. I was quoting the law. I wasn't suggesting to the witness anything about the investigations or anything like that. If you would know the Law on Criminal Procedure, you wouldn't have asked such a thing. But I was quoting the law. And I asked the comment of the witness. So, therefore, I wasn't suggesting anything of -- concerning the investigations because it is known, Your Honours, who is in charge of the investigation and who conducts what, in accordance with the criminal procedure which is -- existed in the former Yugoslavia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, two points. First of all, I'm quoting directly from Mr. Zecevic's question which was really an assertion. And secondly, I think we're entitled to know what the reality of the situation was back in 1992 as his question clearly suggested that there's a need to explore this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would -- I would welcome if I could get the reference for -- for my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 4 of today's transcript. It's right at the end of page 4, beginning of page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If properly understood, Mr. Olmsted's question is, notwithstanding the law and the context of the law, what was the reality on the ground. I think it's a permissible question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, I'll ask it again. When a prosecutor -- back in 1992, if a prosecutor heard a rumour that a crime was committed, did the prosecutor have the resources, the means, to conduct his or her own investigation into that potential crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law specified Article 153, or perhaps 151, paragraph 2, I can't remember now, that if a prosecutor received a rumour, then he could act on his own or act through organs of the interior. However, according to the old Law on Criminal Procedure, the prosecutor could never act on his own. He always had to act either through police organs or authorised officials or through judges or state organs. And the prosecutor could also call in the person filing the criminal report. Otherwise, the prosecutor could never do anything on his own, as is possible now, under the law. In paragraph 1, it says that the organs of the interior are duty-bound to act at all times, whereas, for the prosecutor it wasn't possible. There was no instrument allowing the prosecutor to act on his own, to call in witnesses, so summon them for interviews and so on. They couldn't carry out any other activities. They always had to act through other organs, even though the law said otherwise. But prosecutors lacked mechanisms to do that without the assistance of other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but please, Mr. Olmsted, instruct the witness to repeat her question [sic] and slowly -- her answer and slowly, because none of she said was properly recorded, I believe. Because she was speaking so fast I couldn't follow in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, the -- you would have heard what Mr. Zecevic has said and just -- just to remind you, everything has to be interpreted so if you could pace your -- your responses so that we can all keep up. And perhaps for clarity, Mr. Olmsted, you better -- you -- you should ask the question again and allow the witness to repeat her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, if you could just repeat your answer with regard to the resources that the prosecutor had back in 1992 to conduct an investigation on his or her own.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
