utterances.text: In 1992, as well as prior to that, even though the Law on Criminal Procedure says that the prosecutor can, on his own, via organs of the interior, via investigative judge or other organs, carry out investigative activities, the prosecutor himself had no instruments available to him to do it on his own. He always had to act via these organs. He had to act via organs of the interior, state organs, or investigating judges or he could also summon the person filing the criminal report for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have up on the screen P1318.23.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you recall, Mr. Zecevic showed you this document earlier today. It's the report on activities of the Ministry of Justice and Administration in May through October 1992 period dated 16 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, unfortunately, I can't read Cyrillic. But I think it's the third paragraph, not the second one which is relatively short but the third one which reads: "The activities of judicial organs so far have not been sufficient particularly regarding the newly established organs. We face the fact that a large number of criminal acts have been carried out in the Republika Srpska. Official organs have filed a small number of criminal reports to the judicial organs." Ms. Gacinovic, based on your own experience back in 1992, did you experience something similar where you were receiving a relatively, very small number of cases being filed with the prosecutor's offices?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honours. It has to be compared to something. I mean -- because it is only logical that the -- the -- that the office of the prosecutor receives the criminal complaints where the criminal act occurs so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted, that -- that's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, compared to what you have learned subsequently over the years with regard to what was happening in that region, the types of crimes that were being committed, you mentioned in 1998 you learned about a number of crimes, do you agree --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you should have anticipated that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to clarify something that Mr. Zecevic also raised during his cross-examination, and this was at page 15. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we have the witness's statement on the screen. This would be 10530. And if we can turn in the original document to page 12. That would be the English version. And then in the B/C/S version, if we could turn to page 20. I'm interested in paragraph 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you may recall, Ms. Gacinovic, that Mr. Zecevic was asking you some questions regarding the Kajtez case, and he put to you that the entry in the log-book pertained to the transfer of the case from the civilian prosecutor's office to the military prosecutor's office. And I'd like you to look at paragraph 62 and see if that refreshes your recollection as to what the entry, KT entry 2294, in fact specified.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I think the clarification I want to make is, in fact, the 1994 KT log-book specified that the case was transferred from the military court to the civilian prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There -- then there has to be some kind of misunderstanding between -- or there is misinformation stated in -- in -- in the -- in the document which was given to us yesterday, which is the additional information -- additional addendum to the 2nd of June 2010 witness statement. It concerns the -- the Appendix 18, question number 4. It's -- I'm not sure which -- which page it is. It is -- it is concerning the -- the log-book of the -- of Sanski Most prosecutor -- or basic prosecutor's office and may this be shown to the witness for explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. I think this will be helpful for the Defence to understand better how to read these tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, if you could turn to the revised Annex 18, table 4. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the first column is -- for the first entry which is the one we're concerned it, it has the number KT 22/94. That's a reference to the 1994 KT log-book for Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, two -- the third column it says: "Court log-book entry number." And it says: "Military prosecutor's office, Banja Luka." Is that where this particular report came from? Or, in other words, that's where the prosecutor's office received that file?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- it follows from the log-book that, in the basic public prosecutor's office of Sanski Most, the case was filed under KT 22/94, and it was received from the military prosecutor's office, Banja Luka. The file reference is VTK-461/92. I concluded from that that the basic public prosecutor's office in Sanski Most received it from the military prosecutor's office. But I was unable to tell to which military prosecutor's's office it was forwarded because the only entry that we see here is from whom it was received and what the registration number or the entry number was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness gave the answer -- the -- the different answer than it was recorded on page 50, line 12, what she was unable to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you just repeat for us what you were not able to tell from the log-book.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell -- or, rather, I could tell that the file arrived at the basic prosecutor's office in Sanski Most from the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. But I was unable to tell whether the case was opened by the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, or possibly another police station sent it to Banja Luka and Banja Luka forwarded it to Sanski Most. I believe that is clear. And I was unable to tell from this who the injured parties are. That's why I stated several persons and that's why it is included in table 4. Because, it is possible that the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka opened the file, but it is also possible that a police station or another natural or legal person opened the file against Danilusko Kajtez. That's how things stand under the law, so I was unable to tell from the log-book who drew up the criminal report. I could only conclude that the criminal report was filed against Danilusko Kajtez, that it was received by the public prosecutor's office in Sanski Most, and that it was entered as entry number KT 22/94, and that it was received from the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka, where the number is VTK 461 and that there are several injured parties. So we know about the type of offence and when it was committed. That's why it is included in table 4. I hope that it was clear this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just another intervention in the transcript, 51, 5 and 6. Just for the consistency of the -- of the transcript, it says here opened the file against Danilusko Kajtez. I believe so far we translated as filing a criminal report or filing a criminal complaint. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think this -- this is matter has been well-covered now so I think we can move on to something new.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Zecevic showed you Article 119 of the SFRY Criminal Code, the one pertaining to serving with the enemy army. Do you recall that? I'm not going to put that up on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now yesterday Judge Harhoff asked you to shed some light on these kinds of cases that were filed in Teslic in 1992, and I want to endeavour to try to do that by first turning to the Teslic KT log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can have that on the screen. It's P1365. And I'm interested in page 4 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. And I think we need to zoom in on entry 126. Yes, that's -- that's the one right there, 126.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see the first three perpetrators in what you'll see is to be a six-perpetrator case. Can you just tell us quickly the ethnicity of these three perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by their first and last names, I can conclude that they were Muslims. Rifat Sahic, Asim Isic, Rasid Isic, as far as I'm able to read the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can look over to the column where it lists the charge that they have been accused of. Actually, please don't scroll over. You can see it from where it is. Can you tell us, what were they charged with?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we could scroll over for me to see if they are indicted or perhaps another ruling was adopted in this case. Can we scroll right a bit more? I can't see the top of the column. Yes, this is good. I think that these cases were forwarded to the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can scroll back down. Yeah, we don't need to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is it possible -- can we look at the column. Is it -- scroll over now. Scroll over. It's difficult to read, but is it possible they were -- they were transferred to the higher prosecutor in Banja Luka, the superior prosecutor in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the superior prosecutor's office was authorised to act only in second-instance proceedings under the -- after the amendments of the law. On 14 December 1992, the basic public prosecutor's office had jurisdiction over all criminal offences. My conclusion would sooner be that the case was transferred to the military prosecutor's office because crimes under Article 119 and others fall under the jurisdiction of military prosecutor's offices, that is, military courts actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to get back to my original question which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it's time for the break. So that if this is a convenient point ... Ms. Gacinovic, when there's a document up on the screen, I'm asked to remind you that if you put your finger on the screen, you would be zooming in continuously on the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we take the break now, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And just so you know, I am nearing my end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're still looking at P1365 which is the 1992 Teslic KT log-book and I don't want to spend much more time on this particular document. But, Ms. Gacinovic, if you can look at column 9 for entry 126.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in a little bit into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I just want you to confirm what they were charged with, these three Muslims: Rifat Sahic, Asim Isic and others.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It follows from the log-book that a criminal report was filed against them, and that it was entered under KT 126, and that the grounds for the criminal report are Articles 119 and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the other reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Criminal Code of the SFRY. The criminal report was filed on the 25th of May, 1992, but it seems that the file was forwarded to the military prosecutor's office. However, at that time, the higher prosecutor's office did not have jurisdiction over such offences. They were under the jurisdiction of the basic prosecutor's office. The higher prosecutor's office could only act in second instance cases. However from the entry here, I cannot tell whether an indictment was issued against these three persons. I believe that crimes that fall under Article 119 and 124, it was the military courts that had jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the third column, I just want to you take note, the KU or the police crime register number for this criminal report is 108; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 108 and the date is 16 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There are three more --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could just flip ahead two pages, just to show that there are three more perpetrators. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the top, we see the three other perpetrators of this Article 119 crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 10531.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What we have before us is a criminal report submitted by the chief of the SJB Teslic to the Teslic public prosecutor's office dated 16 June 1992, and we see at the top there's an entry or is handwritten there a KU number, 108. Can you confirm that this is the criminal report for the entry we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can just take a look at the information regarding the perpetrators. Can you tell us, the alleged perpetrators, where were they from in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the personal information about the indictees, we can see that they all have permanent resident at Gornji Rankovic which is in the municipality of Teslic, except for one who it says now is a fugitive, but even he has permanent residence at Gornji Rankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, there is not an indictment, this is a criminal report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a criminal report submitted by the SJB of Teslic to the basic public prosecutor's office in Teslic, and it was entered into the KT log-book, as we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is typical of criminal reports, but it also lists, in addition to the names of the perpetrators, or alleged perpetrators and where they are from but where they are employed, and in this case where it is indicated, it shows that these individuals were unemployed at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In criminal reports when they are submitted by the police or the police either in police station or in Security Services Centre, it is -- it was usual to mention the basic personal information about the -- all the persons mentioned therein. The date of birth, the place of person -- permanent residence, the names of their parents, their occupation, where they work, et cetera. It is also mentioned what they're being charged with and what evidence has been collected until that time that corroborate the allegations that they have committed the crime they are charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if the perpetrators were members of the military, this is also where that would be specified?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the police draws up a criminal report, it mentions the basic information. They needn't mention everything. But the prosecutor does have, when he or she issues an indictment. The police always mentions the most important personal information about the persons against whom the criminal report is submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn the page in both the B/C/S and the English. And we can see that these six individuals were accused of digging holes of approximately 1 metre in diametre during the conflict in Gornja Rankovic, based upon the instructions of Suljo Beganovic. Ms. Gacinovic, without more, would this be sufficient grounds to charge someone with an Article 119 crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, I don't know how the witness can answer this question. The fact is that they have been charged or they have been -- the criminal complaint have been filed. I mean, the prosecutor charges by filing the -- the indictment with the charges. So I'm not -- I'm not really sure I follow how would the witness be able to answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm just asking her based on her experience, her long experience as a prosecutor. She sees the facts laid out here in the criminal report filed by the police. Let me make my -- my statement, please. She can read this criminal report for herself, see the facts as laid out by the police in this case and, as a prosecutor with many years, experience, tell us whether this would be sufficient information for her to proceed on an Article 119 case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, had you an objection as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I was asking similar questions to the witness concerning a particular case, the answer was that the reason for her coming here was the work she did and that she cannot comment on a case which wasn't hers and which she isn't familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for that reminder, Mr. Aleksic. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? The question was put to me and I can't seem to get a chance to answer it. If I were to work on this case, I would probably file a request to start collecting statements from the -- these persons pursuant to Article 143. Apart from that, we see here that there -- this is an annex to this letter which is an Official Note. We don't know its content. I cannot tell based on the criminal report itself what to do, but I don't think I could issue an indictment. Only upon perusing the entire case file I would be able to decide. I didn't comment on the work of the prosecutor in question or anybody else but I would either return this to the police to interview the concerned persons or if that had been done, I would have filed a request to launch an investigation. But based on this criminal report alone, I couldn't make a decision whether or not there are sufficient grounds to issue an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is not on our 65 ter list. It has been disclosed to the Defence, I believe in March of this year, so they've had it for quite some time. Prior to yesterday when Judge Harhoff raised some questions regarding these types of cases, we didn't anticipate this would be extremely probative but now having heard some of the questions and some of the issues, we would move to first admit it on to our 65 ter list and then admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Olmsted, as Mr. Aleksic has correctly observed having regard to the purpose for which this witness is called, and it's your case, you're reexamining, why are we going down this path? How does it assist in terms of the -- -- the -- what the evidence -- what the testimony of this witness has been? Why ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to a previous witness where the Defence admitted a number of criminal reports, that witness, ST-210, had never seen before, had no personal knowledge of, it was relevant to put the results of that witness's analysis of the log-books - in that case it was the crime registers - into context. And Judge Harhoff had asked a number of questions trying to understand these -- serving with the enemy army charges that were filed in Teslic, this is just an example of one of them to help the Trial Chamber better understand that issue. So we do think it is a probative document that would be very useful for this Trial Chamber to understand this witness's reports and in particular these types of crimes that were charged in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object, based -- first of all, we know what are the guide-lines is for amending the 65 ter list, and that is -- that is number one. The second, obviously this is the first time the -- the witness sees this. There's no nexus. And the third and the most important, I'm now -- I'm having a problem. I seem not to understand the Prosecutor's case anymore. Maybe -- maybe the Prosecutor can enlighten us what is their case in this respect. This was not -- this -- this wasn't the matter which was in dispute between the party. It was not the issue in the case, as far as I know so far. Now, if the -- Judge Harhoff posed the question, I tried to assist by showing the criminal -- the criminal law of the SFRY in order to explain what the Article 119 is. Now the Prosecutor, for some reason, wants to expand their case in this area. It has not been charged. It has not been in their pre-trial brief. This is the first time we ever hear any -- any talk about this serving -- about this article and serving in the enemy's army, as -- as an issue in this case. So, therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zecevic -- Mr. Zecevic, in all fairness, you were the one who drew the Chamber's attention to Article 119 and that sparked my questions. And -- and the -- the -- the idea of prosecution of civilians who are asked to perform work for the Muslim army, such as digging trenches, still strikes me as surprising. If I were to put an additional question to the witness, that would be whether the witness had any knowledge of any Serbs being prosecuted for a similar crime. But I may get back to the witness on that. But I think that there is some probative value to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, just for the record, I -- it was Your Honour's question to the witness during the -- the direct examination of Mr. Olmsted, and I tried to assist by posing the question for -- because I thought that Your Honours did not understood [sic] her -- her answer, and that is why I brought up the -- the -- the criminal law. It wasn't my intention at all. I tried to be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, as I think is our duty. So, therefore, I didn't raise this issue, and -- and so far, what I'm saying is, so far we are not -- we were not aware that this is a part of the Prosecutor's case. Now, of course, if the Trial Chamber is -- is interested in -- in some of the aspects of this Article 119, and some other things, of course, the witness may answer. But my problem was that Mr. Olmsted is offering a document to be admitted, and I gave my reasons why I object for that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: By majority, the Chamber is of the view that this document is -- should not be admitted as it is irrelevant, dealing with the collateral issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand your ruling, but if I may say one more thing in favour of our position. We have heard evidence from witnesses from this municipality who talk about this very issue of these types of cases being filed in Teslic, why they were filed, what happened to the people who were -- the charges were filed against. So it is relevant in that regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, we have ruled. So we move on, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P1284.07 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is the final topic I want to cover today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honours. I don't see how does this come out of the -- the cross-examination. We never raised the issue of the military courts or the Law on Military Courts. It was the witness's answer which referred to the military courts, but it wasn't raised by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honours, but the Defence, just as the Prosecution, must take the answers that the witness gives to their questions, and I have the right to re-examine a witness on one of her answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that came up in cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me that even if the witness volunteered an answer, since it came out of the cross and it appears to be relevant, you may proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, during cross-examination, you mentioned that the Law on Military Courts specifies when the military courts have jurisdiction over a crime. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page. And focus on Article 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Article 13, we see, enumerates the circumstances in which the military courts have jurisdiction over civilian perpetrators; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I still -- I still don't see what -- what -- I -- if -- if I thought that there was enough foundation to bring this issue to this witness, because this witness is a civilian prosecutor. It is not the military prosecutor. We had the military prosecutors over here, and we have all the answers from the competent person on the record. I -- I -- I really don't see how -- what is the foundation for asking the questions of -- that -- the witness can answer the questions which -- which pertain to her -- her job which is Law on Criminal Procedure and the criminal law but not on the military -- military courts because she was not the military prosecutor or a part of the military judiciary system. Therefore, there is no -- there is -- there's no foundation for -- for asking her, and she's not an expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, before Mr. Zecevic rose, I was about to ask how far are you going with this. Because, as Mr. Zecevic has correctly pointed out, the -- if -- if -- if -- where you now seem to be leading, is to get an opinion from this witness in terms of an area of law which is not her -- within her field of expertise. Then it is obviously irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was interesting objection because the Defence have asked a number of prosecutor's and judges who -- civilian prosecutors and judges who have testified here this very line of questions, and I am simply following suit with this witness. And I think you'll see that I will not take it very far. I just have a few questions regarding this, and it all -- you'll see pertains directly to what she stated during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Olmsted, insofar as if there's a controversy about the effect of a particular law, and the meaning of -- the interpretation of a particular law, isn't the side who is inviting a particular conclusion by the Trial Chamber obliged to call a person who purports to be an expert on the law in question. And the problem with this witness is that the law with which we are presently confronted is not something that she is apparently competent to speak to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, I think that issue that you have raised certainly goes to the weight of the evidence that the witness can give on this issue. Can I ask some foundational questions regarding her familiarity with an interaction with military courts over the years. Obviously there has to be some co-operation between the civilian prosecutor and the military prosecutor when -- as we've seen already with this witness, some cases get transferred to the military prosecutor and vices verse. We saw the Kajtez case where a military case went from the Banja Luka military prosecutor's office or military court and went to the Sanski Most civilian prosecutor's court. So there is an interaction between the military judicial system and the civilian judicial system. But I'm not really asking her questions that would require her expertise. I really -- if I may just ask my next question, I think you will see that it relates to what she told us during her cross-examination. I'm not going to delve deep into this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Ms. Gacinovic, if you can look -- we're still looking at Article 13, but I want you to look at the last paragraph of Article 13, which states that: "The military court try prisoners of war for any committed criminal act and for crimes against humanity and international law." Is that the provision that you were referring to during cross-examination as to when the military courts have jurisdiction over such crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This provision of Article 13 - I don't know which paragraph - is quite clear; namely that military courts have jurisdiction over all crimes committed by prisoners of war as well as crimes against humanity and international law under Articles 141 to 155 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. And I said something very similar when I looked at that case from 1992. I said that it was the military prosecutor's office which had jurisdiction over that case because we saw earlier that Article 119 specified that the military court had jurisdiction over those cases. So if the persons filing the criminal report concluded that it was the military court that had jurisdiction for a particular case, then the entire file would be sent to the military court. And similar applies in this particular case. If it was a crime for which military courts had jurisdiction, then the case would be sent to the relevant competent military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I refer Your Honours to paragraph 13 to her 2 June 2010 statement for further explanation of this. Once -- if it is admitted into evidence to save some time here. And at this stage, I have no further questions. And if the -- Your Honours don't have any questions, I would move to admit her 92 ter package which would include the addendum to her 2 June 2010 statement, that's 65 ter 10530, into evidence. So that would be 10527, 10528, 10529 and 10530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm glad Mr. Olmsted reminded Your Honours to paragraph 13 of the -- of the statement which he is now trying to introduce into the -- the evidence, and it is quite in contradiction with witness said just a couple of minutes ago, looking at the -- at the actual law, so I ... I'm not sure what is the position of the -- of the Office of the Prosecutor in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think it is consistent, but I could bring it up and have her confirm what she states in paragraph 13 of her 2 June 2010 statement. She is stating that the military courts had jurisdiction when it was a military person, obviously, and as well as if the -- the perpetrator was a prisoner of war. She's distinguishing when the civilian courts have jurisdiction or when the civilian prosecutor would have jurisdiction. And she covers this not only in that paragraph but throughout her statement. She notes where the civilian prosecutor's office had particular cases that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To the extent there may be an inconsistency, isn't this a matter that we would deal with at the end of the day. It isn't something that we need concern ourselves with at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have a question about not to -- of the witness but Mr. Olmsted. You mentioned four documents in the 92 ter package -- and going till 105030 and what 105031? If I'm not wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is it 10531 the one that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 10531, I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We'd move to admit that one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Pardon? That's the one we refuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's the one you refuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry about that. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam, just to round this issue up about the crime which we have dealt with here most recently, you may already have told us but it just slipped my attention. And my question is: Can you offer an explanation as to why this case about the six Muslim gentlemen who were charged for violation of Article 119 for having drug trenches for the Muslim army, you told us that this would been a military -- a case for the military court, yet it ended up before the civilian court or the civilian police. Why was that; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts be put back up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. If it will help the Trial Chamber. Let me look at the -- the -- the exhibit number. I don't think there is any question that Article 119 cases fell within the jurisdiction of the military court, to save some time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That was clear. But it just appeared to me that this particular case ends up before the civilian authorities, and I just wasn't sure of how that happened. If it was originally a case for the military police and the military court, then why did it end up before the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA GACINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the log-book. I concluded that it didn't end up with civilian courts. The proceedings were begun but it is possible that the Law on Military Courts was not in force yet, and as soon as it entered into force, it was the military court and the military prosecutor who had jurisdiction. Based on the log-book, I would say that it was sent to the military prosecutor's office. Article 13 lists specifically in which cases when perpetrators are civilians would the military courts have jurisdiction and that includes crimes under Article 119. Based on the log-book, we can see that in December 1992, the case file was sent to the relevant military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. I didn't catch that during the course of events, and I apologise. And thank you for your answer. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the 92 package is admitted. And, Ms. Gacinovic, We thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honours. The 92 ter package 65 ter 10527 will be Exhibit P1609.1, 65 ter 10528 will be Exhibit P1609.2, 65 ter 10529 will be P1609.3, and 65 ter 10530 will be P1609.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Pidwell will be leading the next witness, so if I may excuse myself so she may occupy my seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may withdraw, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I informed that I would have one so-called housekeeping matter before the witness is brought in, so if I may at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we received yesterday's decision about the -- the -- the experts, the Office of the Prosecutor experts. Now we were told by our friends from the -- from the Office of the Prosecutor side is that according to the plan, they -- they intend to call expert Ewan Brown, the military expert for the Office of the Prosecutor between 20th and the 22nd of October. Your Honours, if I may remind Your Honours, on the 26th of September, on pages 14087, 088, and further 14152, 153, we made the -- it's -- it's -- I believe it's the 2nd of September, I'm sorry, I mispronounced the date. We made the submission concerning our problems with the disclosure of the Mladic material. Now, the Mladic material has been disclosed to us last -- the Friday before the last, so immediately before our site visit. Your Honours, myself, I am -- I am the one who will be cross-examining the -- Ewan Brown expert for the Office of the Prosecutor, but due to reasons which are beyond my control, Mr. O'Sullivan and myself are -- are flying to Canada on a mission for preparation of our case tomorrow, and we will not be here for the whole week. And there -- there wasn't anything we could do about it because I have to apply for the visas with the Canadian authorities and they gave me a certain date when I can enter Canada for once and that's it. Therefore, we have to leave -- we have to leave tomorrow. Your Honours, having in view the amount of the material which has been disclosed to us from the Mladic diaries and the relevance of that material for the cross-examination of Ewan Brown, the -- the military expert, I can -- I can inform the Trial Chamber that we are not going to be ready to cross-examine him on the 20 -- on -- on these date, 20th or 22nd of October. We suggested to our friends from the Prosecution that the only other option that -- that we see is that they call this witness at the end of their case. Because, Your Honours, on the 2nd of September, we asked -- I asked myself for two weeks' adjournment in order to be able to deal with this -- this amount of material from the Mladic diaries. And if I may remind the Trial Chamber, in all other case in this Tribunal, the adjournment of at least two weeks was giving [sic] to the parties to get -- to read and analyse the material of Mladic diaries. I -- I'm afraid to suggest that now, because I see Your Honours' determination to keep on the pace as scheduled, but I would -- I -- I -- I felt it was my obligation to -- to put the Trial Chamber on notice of the problem that we are having. Because, definitely, what I can say at this point is we are not going to be able to prepare the cross-examination for this witness by the -- by the end of October. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, am I wrong by thinking that your request that you withdrew your request for two weeks stay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I'm just -- I'm just not repeating it. It's on the record, and I stick to it, but I'm not repeating it because I'm pretty sure if I would repeat it now, the Trial Chamber will not grant that request. That is my opinion, with all due respect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, are you counsel with responsibility for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Kind of, Your Honour. I can address you on this point. Good evening. Firstly, if I can kindly request the Defence to raise these procedural matters at the end of the day, rather than the time when we got a witness waiting outside, in the future, I would appreciate that. Secondly, the -- this matter was discussed approximately a month ago, and the -- to give you a little bit of a chronology, there's two issues here. There's the Mladic notebooks which have been ruled upon and there's the audio files and video files. We disclosed the notebooks and 68 audios on the 23rd of July. That was the first portion of the audios which had been processed through the OTP. There was a second batch which comprised 52 audio and video recordings which were disclosed to the Defence on the 15th of September. Now accompanying that disclosure of the 52 audios and videos was a spreadsheet, an internal Office of the Prosecutor spreadsheet, which had a summary of each and every audio from not only those 52 but the 68 previously disclosed advising the Defence, well, it was an OTP product, but advising the contents of the tape. Some of them are birthday parties, some of them are French lessons, some of them are meetings, and so we have done a revision and that spreadsheet has been disclosed to the Defence to assist them in reviewing this material. Of the audios and videos that we have reviewed, we have identified two audios and one video which we consider possibly could fall within Rule 66(B), not 58, possibly within Rule 66(B), if it is interpreted widely. And we identified these when they were disclosed and this information was passed on to the Defence. We did not consider that they needed to disclose the others, because we didn't consider they fell with any of the Rules but we did upon their request. This should not be grounds for an adjournment when we have disclosed information to them upon their request, which, in our view, is not relevant to this case, but they seem to be wanting to use this as a method to extend the -- well, prolong the testimony -- the -- the length of case or not have this expert appear. If we go back, Your Honour, every single expert that we've scheduled to testify in this case we have he had to move because the Defence have not been ready at the first moment that we're scheduled them to testify. This expert is our second-to-last one, and to coin a phrase, he cannot be moved from the schedule. Even if we put him at the end of the case and we are currently looking at the -- if we don't have to -- well, the 92 bis witnesses aside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may interrupt and inquire, Ms. Pidwell, can -- if he -- although he can't be moved, can he be divided in terms of separating his cross-examination, postponing that to a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If the later date is the new year, then the answer is yes. We anticipate finishing our current witness list at the end of November. But he cannot be brought forward. He has obligations which cannot be shifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Pidwell, the -- assuming that there not been this indication of the problems of the Prosecution had, according -- the Defence had, according to the witness's convenience how long was he scheduled to be here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: He is scheduled to be here for three days, so he would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would that have been sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Well, to testify, sorry, in court. His court time would be three days and we would bring him on a weekend and anticipate that he would leave on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking, whether the three days that he was booked to be here whether that would be sufficient to cover his testimony in its entirety, in any event.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We hope so. That's the estimate that we've been provided -- for the cross-examination estimate that has been provided to us from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours, as -- as Ms. Pidwell says, this is what -- this was the estimate. After we reviewed the Mladic books we might -- we might ask for additional time to -- to cross-examine this witness. That is the precisely the point which I'm trying to -- to explain to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There is just one additional point for Your Honours consideration. My learned friend said that in other Trial Chambers, the Defence have been given adjournments for approximately two weeks to review this material. It's correct that some Prosecution teams have been given adjournment to review the Mladic diaries or notebooks, but in my -- on my information that I have, I don't understand any trial teams or Defence teams have been given additional adjournment time to review the audiotapes which have been subsequently disclosed and the notebooks were disclosed way back in April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, to minimise any further inconvenience to the witness waiting outside, we have heard the Defence's application -- not an application, but we have heard the comments that both sides have made and it's something that we -- we're obviously going have to consider outside of court. And if we need further information from counsel, we would revert to you. So could we have the witness who is waiting in, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution calls Witness ST-184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, is he -- is he a viva voce witness for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, he was -- he was one who was subject to our discussion and your ruling a couple of days ago. We had asked -- he was previously 92 ter. We switched him over to viva voce because of the problems with the audiotaped interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, than means six hours for the Prosecution; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Except I don't anticipate taking that long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the Defence will take how long, Mr. Zecevic, for this witness, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe my friend, Mr. Cvijetic informs me that we will take one session, maybe two hours at the maximum, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we indicate 2 hours, but I think it may be less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. First of all, to you hear me in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that a solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now, then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may sit down. And, sir, could we begin by asking to you state your full name, your date and place of birth please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Simo Miskovic, born on the 7th of March, 1945, in the village of Donji Ratkovo, Kljuc municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your today's profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been retired for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 20 years. So you were already retired in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I retired in 1991, starting on the 1st of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this your first testimony before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before any court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Before any court, okay. Let me then explain you briefly how the procedure will go on in this Tribunal. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution who is sitting on your right, and the Prosecution has asked for, all together, six hours to examine you in-chief. After that, counsel for Mr. Stanisic, sitting on your left, has asked for more or less two-hours to cross-examine you. And when Mr. Zecevic is through, the cross-examination by Mr. Krgovic for Mr. Zupljanin will more or less take two hours equally. After that, the Prosecution will have the floor again for -- to put some more questions to you in re-examination, and the Judges could have questions of you as well. As a practical matter, we sit in the afternoon until 7.00, starting at a quarter to 2.00. And in the morning, if we sit in the morning, we sit from 9.00 to a quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon, we start quarter past 2.00. But we all only sit mornings or afternoons, never the both. So one other matter, we take breaks for technical reasons. Tapes for the audio have to be changed, and so on. We take breaks every 90 minutes. If for any reason, for any reason you should need an extra break at any time, please let us know and we will accommodate you. That's what I had to say. I thank you very much. And I give the floor to Ms. Pidwell for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, we heard you say that you were born in the municipality of Kljuc. Where were you raised?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: My father was a police officer, so after the Second World War he had to move around. For a while, I lived at Sanski Most where he was transferred. After that, he was transferred to Kozarac, where he was chief of the police station. We lived in Kozarac, and I attended second -- through the seventh form of primary school there. After that, my father was transferred to Prijedor, where we have lived since 1957.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after you completed your schooling, you then did your compulsory military training, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was compulsory for all able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after that, you commenced a nine-month police course in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after completing that course, you then commenced work as a police officer in Banja Luka and remained there from 1968 to 1973; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. From 8 January 1968 through 1 April 1973, when I was transferred to Prijedor to the same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what position was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a police officer. First a police constable. Then I worked in the crime police -- crime prevention, that is, after which I became a squad commander at Omarska, and later I was a police commander at the centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were the squad commander in Omarska from 1978 to 1992. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And from 1982, you were the Deputy Commander in the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: 1992, oh, no, no, actually 1982. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And from 1982 until your retirement in January 1991, you remainder in the Prijedor police.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was Deputy Commander of the -- the police, and I mean the general police, because there was also the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And at the date of your retirement, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the police station was Fikret Kadiric [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall who the chief of the police -- the Prijedor police was at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment -- well, I can't really remember. No, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I don't think it's a contention issue, if I suggest a name. Hasan Telundzic, would that refresh your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that he came later. After the multi-party elections, I think. But I wasn't with the police anymore, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So you retired shortly after the multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the end of 1990. As of 1 January 1991, I was a pensioner already.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, during your time working in Banja Luka, did you know the accused Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think that he had started his police career then.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, if I could have you look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's P1526.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You'll see -- it will come up on your screen in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's a general map of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. With all local communities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Would you agree that the town of Prijedor is the largest settlement in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And on that map, we have a -- what looks like a railway line running through approximately half of the municipality. Was there a railway line that connected the town of Prijedor to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That railroad line was built long ago. I think it was in Austro-Hungarian times. It runs from Bosanski Novi through Prijedor, Banja Luka, and it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the main road south east of Prijedor follows largely the course of that railway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: That road was built in the early 1970s. Before that time there was an old unpaved road which ran through Kozarsko Zavosko [phoen] Kozarac, and so on, Kamcani and on toward Ivanska. It was an unpaved road. Whereas the tarmac road which runs parallel to the railroad line was only built in the early 1970s.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, before the multi-party elections in 1990, would you agree that there was ethnic tolerance in the municipality of Prijedor, that there were mixed marriages and friendships and it was a peaceful co-existence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a fact. It was like that in all of Yugoslavia, including Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just looking at this map again, sir, you've got there's some towns marked on it. And perhaps can you use that to assist in describing the police substations that were -- existed in Prijedor, or exist in Prijedor. We know about the main Prijedor station which is located in Prijedor town. But can you please describe the -- where the other station -- substations were located?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, we called them branch police stations. They were branches of the police stations proper. They could be found at Omarska and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name of the other place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreters didn't quite get the last town that you mentioned where the police branch was located. They caught Omarska but not the other one.

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Kozarac and Omarska, whereas Ljubija was a police station but later it -- it became a branch station. That is -- which is a unit at lower level.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say it's a unit at a lower level, does that mean that it is essentially a reserve police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. The police stations were in Ljubija and in Prijedor, whereas, the branch police stations or substations, as you call them, are branches of the Central Station, whereas Ljubija was a -- an autonomous police station, but due to the small population and the absence of greater problems, they were reduced to a branch station. They were no longer a police station proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, can you please explain the -- what I will call Prijedor 2 station, where you subsequently became the commander in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first, you must understand the organisational structure in that Yugoslavia. In socialist Yugoslavia, both in the military and the police, there were active police stations and reserve police stations. They also had a wartime assignment. Everybody had a wartime assignment, some with the police and some with the military. So the police had their reserve force and, of course, the army did as well. And that is unrelated to the peacetime structure and organisation. In those stations, people were trained because they had other peacetime jobs, and only in case of need they could be called up to perform police duties and everybody knew their wartime assignment where they were supposed to work in case of war. These are the wartime police stations, reserve police stations which didn't function daily as the regular ones that operated 24/7.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So Prijedor 2 which was stationed at -- well, where was that stationed when it was activated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: It's at Urija, above the railroad line and the highway. It's actually a suburban settlement which now has grown, but it used to be a smaller settlement. Nowadays, it is part of the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the area that the Prijedor 2 police station covered when it was activated was what?

utterances.speaker: SIMO MISKOVIC
utterances.text: Not only when it was activated, they already had their wartime assignment and the territory where they had jurisdiction was defined. And that territory was mostly Brezicani, Cejreci, Puharska, Palanciste, and those areas above the railroad line. But there was also the police station Kozarac which covered that territory and another in Ljubija which had jurisdiction over another territory and so on. Apart from the active police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I wonder if that's a convenient time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Miskovic, we have reached the point at which we must adjourn for the day. We will resume in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00 when your testimony will continue. Having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side in this matter; and in such conversations as you may have with persons outside the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we rise now, to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 1st of October, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
